DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26

## Summary verdict

The descriptive data are useful, and rolling out reminders more widely may well be sensible. But the report's central claim, that reminders *caused* a 13-point rise in uptake, is not supported by its own evidence. The headline overall uptake figure is also arithmetically wrong. Both need fixing before this goes to the Health and Wellbeing Board.

## 1. The overall uptake figure is wrong, and Eastvale did not reach 65%

Table 1's "All schools" row gives 13,772 vaccinated out of 22,080 eligible. That is **62.4%**, not 66.0%. The row components add up correctly (9,120 + 12,960 = 22,080; 6,384 + 7,388 = 13,772), so only the percentage is wrong. It is not a simple average of the two groups either, which would be 63.5%.

This removes the claim in Section 3, repeated in your note, that Eastvale passed the national 65% ambition "for the first time". On these figures it fell about 2.6 points short. Please trace where 66.0% came from and correct Section 3 and the table. Overall consent return was 67.1% (14,810 / 22,080), which may be the source of the confusion.

The group-level figures check out: 75.0% and 61.5% consent return, 70.0% and 57.0% uptake, and 93.3% and 92.7% vaccinated given consent.

## 2. The 13-point gap is not a clean comparison and cannot be read as the effect of reminders

Your note calls this "a clean side-by-side comparison". It isn't, and the report's own Background section explains why. Schools chose whether to opt in, and those that did were very different:

- **School nurses:** 29 of 38 reminder schools (76%) had a full-time nurse, against 11 of 54 non-reminder schools (20%). A nurse chasing consent forms could plausibly account for much of a consent-return gap on its own.
- **Affluence and geography:** reminder schools were concentrated in the more affluent west. Uptake is strongly linked to deprivation nationally.
- **Population:** Section 4 notes that non-reminder schools have more families speaking languages other than English and higher household mobility. Both independently depress consent return.

So the 13 points is a mix of any reminder effect plus the nurse, affluence and population differences. The true reminder effect could be close to 13 points, but it could also be close to zero. Section 3's statement that the gap "shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points" and Section 6's "Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points…" both need to be withdrawn or heavily qualified. The comparison with "any other intervention we have tried" is also unsupported, since no comparable estimate for other interventions is presented.

## 3. Reminders cannot reach many of the families in non-reminder schools

Section 4 contains the strongest reason to doubt the 57% → 70% projection:

- **Mobile coverage:** only 61% of families in non-reminder schools have a valid mobile number on record, against 93% in reminder schools. About 39% of non-consenting families (roughly 1,950 pupils' families) could not receive a text at all.
- **Language:** the messages and portal are presumably English-only. Families who speak another language at home may not act on them even if they receive them.
- **Incomplete forms:** paper forms in these schools often come back with the medical history section blank. A reminder to return a form does nothing about this. Please clarify whether incomplete forms count as "consent returned" in Table 1.

Even if reminders had a true 13-point effect in the west, the same intervention would reach fewer people in the east and convert fewer of them. The projection to 70% assumes the effect transfers unchanged to the population least able to receive it. Read together, Sections 4 and 6 contradict each other.

## 4. The cost analysis is accurate but slightly overstated

The arithmetic holds:

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| 4,990 × 3 × £0.08 | £1,198 |
| 2,280 × 3 × £0.08 | £547 |
| Set-up | £2,500 |
| **Total** | **£4,245** |

Two small points:

- The figures count pupils without consent, not families. Siblings mean the family count is lower.
- Families with no valid mobile number cannot be sent texts.

Both make the real cost lower, so "under £5,000" is safe. However, the low cost is not a reason to believe the effect is large. It is a reason the intervention is low-risk to try, which is a different argument and a fair one.

## 5. Alternatives are underexplored

The report has some evidence on another option. Mop-up sessions add an estimated 3–6 points but ran in only 14 schools because of staffing. That is a more direct lever for the eastern schools than texts that many families can't receive. The report should also consider:

- improving mobile number data in eastern schools;
- translated messages and forms;
- help with completing the medical history section.

Each of these targets a barrier the report itself identifies.

## 6. How to get a credible estimate

Some of this can be done with data you already have:

1. **Prior-year comparison (difference-in-differences):** compare 2024-25 and 2025-26 uptake in the same schools. If reminder schools were already about 13 points ahead before reminders, the effect is close to zero. This is the single most useful extra analysis.
2. **Matched comparison:** compare reminder and non-reminder schools with similar nurse provision and deprivation (for example, the 9 reminder schools without a nurse against the 43 non-reminder schools without one).
3. **Within-school timing:** in reminder schools, check whether consents arrive in spikes after each text, and how many come through the portal link.
4. **Staggered rollout for 2026-27:** if you extend reminders, phase them in across schools in a random order. That would give a genuinely clean estimate at almost no extra cost.

## Suggested changes to the recommendation

Funding reminders for all schools is defensible because they are cheap. But the report should:

- correct the overall uptake to 62.4% and remove the "above 65%" claim;
- describe the 13-point gap as an association that is confounded by nurse provision and affluence;
- drop the projection that uptake will rise from 57% to 70%;
- pair reminders with work on mobile data, translation and mop-up capacity in the eastern schools;
- build an evaluation design into the 2026-27 rollout, not just a year-end uptake report.

On your note's point that you "looked hard for reasons not to scale this and have not found any": the case for scaling is reasonable on cost grounds. The case that scaling alone will close the east–west gap is where the report's own Sections 2 and 4 raise the strongest objections.
